name: Warda Ahmed's research is changing how patients recover

content.title: Warda Ahmed's research is changing how patients recover
content.summary: Warda is a soon to be graduate driven by curiosity and a passion for neuroscience

media.alt: Warda Ahmed's research is changing how patients recover

content.text: Pakistan needs more people like Warda Ahmed in its health care system - the kind who pause to understand how things work, notice where they don't, and quietly begin to fix them. Almost like a mechanic, except her tools are not nuts and bolts, but the human body and the systems designed to heal it.

When Warda entered AKU's medical school in Pakistan, she did not arrive with a fixed plan. What she did have was curiosity and a natural instinct for problem solving. Through the breadth of exposure she encountered at Aga Khan University, she gradually found her specific niche of interest in neurosurgery, a field that demanded both precision and creativity. Along the way, she developed a passion for research, one that allowed her to ask not just what we do in medicine, but why we do it that way, and whether it could be done better.

Early in her time at AKU, Warda began working on a project with several national and international mentors. What started as a routine study grew, over three years, into a global collaborative spanning 81 countries. It was her first glimpse into how local inquiry and silent persistence could carry global relevance.

She later joined the research arm of AKU's Surgery Interest Group, eventually becoming its Vice President. There, she found what she describes as a family of students and faculty mentors. Over three years, the group generated more than 400 student research opportunities and contributed to a total of 10 publications.

Her own research focuses on clinically meaningful questions, often using large datasets to examine how procedures work and how small changes can affect patient outcomes over time. That mindset led to one of her most significant researhc highlights. While studying decompressive craniectomy for traumatic brain injury, she noticed that standard practice required patients to undergo two surgeries. She explored an alternative, the hinge technique, which eliminates the need for a second operation. Patients recovered faster, and the technique was equally effective to the standard procedure, all while reducing costs and strain on health care systems. In countries like Pakistan, these differences matter immensely.

Encouraged by her mentors, Warda presented her findings at an international conference during an elective at Emory University. She was the only medical student in the room, the youngest, and the only participant from Pakistan. Her work was well-received and much appreciated by surgeons there who prompted her to share it more widely.

By the end of her third year, Warda had led three major collaborative studies. As she graduates, she has contributed to over 20 publications and presented at more than 10 national and international conferences. She credits her confidence to AKU's culture of inquiry and mentorship. "The research here solves real problems," she says. "It's not just for our CVs. It really makes you want to give back."
